This lesson was written by the Atomic teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 12: Renewable and Non-Renewable Energy Resources.
Solar panels use photovoltaic cells: particles of light, called photons,
knock electrons out of atoms, making an electric current.
It's clean and renewable.
But which energy resources are truly sustainable?
An energy resource is anything from which we can get energy.
Wood can be burnt to release its stored chemical energy as heat.
Others include fossil fuels like coal and oil, gases, nuclear fuels like uranium,
biofuels, and electricity stored in cells.
Every part of society needs energy: homes for heating, lighting and cooking; transport;
industry; computers and data centres; farming; and healthcare.
Most of the energy we use is in the form of electricity.
Imagine life without a reliable energy supply: homes go dark,
factories stop and the economy suffers.
Today we use more technology, and so more energy, than ever before.
Energy is needed in every part of daily life.
Here are four places that depend on a reliable supply.
At home we use energy for cooking, lighting, heating or cooling rooms,
and charging our phones and laptops.
Buses, cars, trains and planes all need a fuel,
such as petrol or diesel, or electricity stored in batteries.
Hospitals need power all day and night.
Many have back-up generators so that life-support machines never stop.
Every message and photo you store online sits in a data centre,
where thousands of computers run and are cooled non-stop.
If the energy supply fails, homes go dark,
transport stops and hospitals rely on back-up power.
Pause and think: which energy resource does your home rely on?
chapters: Real life: where does our energy go?

captions: Fossil fuels formed from the remains of living things,
buried and exposed to intense heat and pressure underground over millions of years.
Coal formed from layers of decayed plant matter and is mined.
Crude oil and natural gas formed mostly from marine
microorganisms and are extracted by drilling deep into rock.
In a power station, fossil fuels are burnt.
The heat turns water into steam, the steam drives turbines,
and the turbines turn generators that produce electricity.
Fossil fuels took millions of years to form,
so they can't be replaced as fast as we use them.
They can only be used once.
That's why they're called non-renewable energy resources.
Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas responsible for global warming,
and toxic pollutants such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides.
Global warming and climate change are linked to more extreme weather: heatwaves, floods,
tropical storms, droughts and wildfires.
Scientists classify these events and map them with keys to plan future action.
Fracking pumps water, sand and chemicals at high
pressure into shale rock to release trapped gas.
It can cause tremors, releases greenhouse and toxic gases,
uses lots of water and makes noise.
And shale gas is still a fossil fuel.
Climate scientists compared the carbon dioxide released for each unit of electricity,
a kilowatt hour, over the whole life of a power station,
from building it to running it.
Coal releases about 820 grams for every kilowatt hour,
and natural gas about 490.
Solar panels release about 48 grams,
while nuclear and wind release only about 12 and 11.
Pause and decide: why do solar,
wind and nuclear still release a little carbon dioxide,
even though nothing is burnt to make the electricity?
Some atoms, like uranium, have a large nucleus.
Fire a neutron at it, and the nucleus splits,
releasing energy and more neutrons.
These split more nuclei in a chain reaction.
This is nuclear fission.
In a nuclear power plant, the heat from fission boils water into steam,
which turns turbines, just as in a coal power station.
Uranium is mined and limited, so nuclear fuel is also non-renewable.
Uranium mining clears land and its waste can pollute water.
Radioactive waste must be stored safely for a very long time.
Hot cooling water harms aquatic life,
and accidents like Chernobyl in 1986 contaminate land for thousands of years.

captions: Renewable energy resources are either in constant supply, like the Sun, wind,
moving water and Earth's heat,
or can be replaced as fast as we use them, like plants.
That makes them sustainable.
Solar energy is free and doesn't pollute when used.
Photovoltaic panels turn light directly into electricity.
Solar thermal plants and solar furnaces use mirrors to focus the Sun's heat,
boiling water to drive turbines.
Molten salt can store the Sun's heat in insulated tanks,
like a battery for solar energy,
so electricity can still be generated after sunset or on a cloudy day.
But solar panels are expensive, sunlight varies and stops at night,
and panels need a lot of land.
Some contain lead and cadmium that can leak, the metals must be mined,
and birds can crash into panels they mistake for lakes.
Two cans hold the same amount of water at 20 degrees Celsius.
One is painted matt black; the other is shiny silver.
Both stand in bright sunshine.
Predict: which water will warm up faster?
Pause and decide.
Watch. After 15 minutes the water in the black can is at 29 degrees,
and in the shiny can it is at 23.
After 30 minutes the black can has reached 38 degrees,
but the shiny can is only at 26.
Explain what you saw.
The matt black surface absorbs most of the Sun's energy,
while the shiny surface reflects much of it away.
That is why solar water heaters on roofs have black pipes and panels.
The energy from the Sun is renewable: it will not run out.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
People have used windmills for centuries to pump water and grind grain.
Today, wind turns giant turbine blades connected to generators,
converting kinetic energy into electricity.
Groups of turbines on land or at sea form wind farms.
Wind energy is clean, releasing nothing harmful into the air.
But turbines are expensive, the wind isn't constant, spinning blades can kill birds,
and turbines can be noisy.
Hydropower uses moving water.
Water held behind a dam is released through turbines, and tides,
waves and ocean currents can turn turbines too.
It's clean, but dams are costly, only work in certain places,
and flood large areas, destroying habitats.
Geothermal energy uses heat from hot rock and magma below Earth's surface.
It heats underground water into steam to turn turbines, or warms buildings directly.
In Iceland, magma is close to the surface, so it's easy to use.
Biomass comes from living things, like wood, crops and animal waste.
It can be burnt, turned into biogas, or made into biofuels like ethanol.
Burning it releases carbon dioxide,
but replanted crops take it back in through photosynthesis.
Biomass is only renewable if it's replaced as quickly as it's used.
Plants can also replace oil in materials: bioplastics are made from corn starch,
seaweed or wood chips.
But some companies exaggerate how green they are, which is called greenwashing.
Now it is your turn to shine!
Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: Why are fossil fuels called non-renewable?
Pause the video now.
Answer: They take millions of years to form and can only be used once.
Question 2: What is nuclear fission?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Splitting a large nucleus, like uranium, to release energy.
Question 3: Name three renewable energy resources.
Pause the video now.
Answer: For example solar, wind, hydropower, geothermal or biomass.
Question 4: Give one environmental drawback of wind turbines.
Pause the video now.
Answer: Blades can kill birds, or turbines cause noise pollution.
